desc: Says whether something exists or not. Also used for having something.
care: 「있다」 covers both existing and owning. You also say 「있어요」 for what you have.

desc: Joins two nouns, or says you did something together with someone. All three mean the same and differ only in tone.
care: 「와/과」 suits writing, 「(이)랑」 suits friends. 「하고」 is safe anywhere.

desc: Marks where something happens, or where it starts from.
care: For a place where an action happens, use 「에서」, not 「에」: 「카페에서 만나요」.

desc: Marks the person you give something to or say something to.
care: Use 「께」 for someone senior. For a thing rather than a person, use 「에」: 「회사에 연락했어요」.

desc: Nothing but that — and it feels like too little.
care: What follows must be negative. 「천 원밖에 있어요」 is wrong.

desc: Compares something to what it resembles.
care: 「같이」 also means 'together', so use 「처럼」 where that could confuse.

desc: Compares two things and says which one is more.
care: 「보다」 attaches to what you compare against. 「어제보다 춥다」 means today is colder.

desc: Every one without exception, or repeating at that interval.
care: 「매일」 is one word and 「날마다」 is a particle. Both are natural.

desc: One or the other — a choice between two actions.
care: To join nouns instead, use 「(이)나」: 「커피나 차」.

desc: The first half and the second half go against each other.
care: The plainest way to contrast two things. It never sounds out of place.

desc: Before that — you do this first.
care: A verb always needs 「-기」: 「먹기 전에」, not 「먹 전에」.

desc: After that thing has finished.
form: N 후에 · V + (으)ㄴ 후에 · same meaning: -(으)ㄴ 다음에
care: A verb takes the past form 「-(으)ㄴ」: 「먹은 후에」, not 「먹는 후에」.

desc: You finish the first thing completely, then do the next.
care: Makes the finishing clearer than plain 「-고」 does.

desc: At that time, or around when that happens.
form: N 때 · A/V + (으)ㄹ 때 · past -았/었을 때
care: After a noun it attaches directly, with no 「-을」: 「방학 때」.

desc: Doing two things at the same time.
form: -면서 after a vowel · -으면서 after a consonant
care: Both halves need the same subject. 「제가 자면서 동생이 공부해요」 is wrong.

desc: The next thing happens the instant the first one ends.
care: For almost no gap in time — much faster than 「-고 나서」.

desc: Throughout that stretch of time.
care: With 「-는 동안」 the two subjects may differ: 「제가 자는 동안 비가 왔어요」.

desc: Says whether you can or cannot do something. Covers both ability and possibility.
form: -ㄹ 수 after a vowel · -을 수 after a consonant
care: Softer than 「못」. To turn something down, 「갈 수 없어요」 is gentler than 「못 가요」.

desc: Asks or tells someone to do something, politely. It also raises the listener.
form: -세요 after a vowel · -으세요 after a consonant
care: A few verbs change entirely: 「먹다」 becomes 「드세요」, 「자다」 becomes 「주무세요」.

desc: Gives a reason. Unlike 「-아/어서」, a request or a suggestion can follow.
form: -니까 after a vowel · -으니까 after a consonant
care: For thanks or apologies use 「-아/어서」: 「와 주셔서 감사합니다」.

desc: Names the cause plainly. Common in writing.
care: No command can follow. Note that 「저 때문에」 means 'my fault', so use it carefully.

desc: You do something with that intention.
form: -려고 after a vowel · -으려고 after a consonant
care: No command or suggestion can follow. Use 「-(으)려면」 or 「-도록」 for that.

desc: Says what the purpose is. It suits writing.
form: N + 을/를 위해서 · V + 기 위해서
care: Stiffer than 「-(으)려고」, which sounds more natural when speaking.

desc: If you intend to do that — and what follows is what it takes.
form: -려면 after a vowel · -으려면 after a consonant
care: Unlike 「-(으)려고」, a command or a suggestion can follow.

desc: You are worried it might turn out that way, so you do something about it first.
form: -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel · -을까 봐 after a consonant
care: What follows is what the worry made you do. Only for bad outcomes.

desc: Even that one — and that is surprising.
form: N + 조차 · usually followed by a negative
care: For taking in even what you would not expect. A negative almost always follows.

desc: On the way there or back.
form: V + 는 길에 · attaches to going and coming verbs
care: Only for verbs of going and coming. 「먹는 길에」 is wrong.

desc: Not the best choice, but that one will do.
form: 이라도 after a consonant · 라도 after a vowel
care: Sounds more considerate than 「(이)나」. Use it when offering something.

desc: You did that, then switched to the opposite.
care: It fits pairs that reverse each other: 「켜다 ↔ 끄다」, 「가다 ↔ 오다」.

desc: You kept doing it, and this is how it turned out.
care: 「-고 보니」 is after finishing once; this one is the result of repeating.

desc: Keep doing it and one day it will turn out that way.
care: 「-다 보니」 already happened; this one is still ahead. Good for encouraging someone.

desc: That one, and nothing else, is the real thing.
form: 이야말로 after a consonant · 야말로 after a vowel
care: Suits writing and speeches. A little heavy for everyday talk.

desc: So that it turns out that way, or right up until then.
care: It also means 'until', as in 「밤새도록」. More formal than 「-게」.

desc: Describes a noun by something that was true once, back then.
care: 「-던」 is for what repeated or was left unfinished; this one finished once.

desc: Supposes that it were so. For things far from what is actually true.
care: 「-(으)면」 is an ordinary condition; this one is an unlikely supposition.

desc: Marks the process or the case of doing something.
care: Unlike the connective 「-는데」, this one is written with a space.

desc: Even supposing that were so, the result does not change.
care: It can also suppose something contrary to fact.

desc: Far from what you expected — the opposite happened instead.
care: A negative follows.

desc: Even the last one left is included.
care: Usually for a situation you regret.

desc: Used to say what something is. Ends in 「이에요」 if the noun has a final consonant, and 「예요」 if it does not.
care: Use 「이에요」 after a final consonant and 「예요」 after a vowel. It is 「친구예요」, not 「친구이에요」.

desc: Korean has two number systems: Sino-Korean (prices, dates, minutes) and native Korean (counting items, age, hours).
form: Sino-Korean: 「일, 이, 삼...」 / Native Korean: 「하나, 둘, 셋...」
care: Before counting units, 「하나, 둘, 셋, 넷」 change to 「한, 두, 세, 네」. Say 「두 잔」, not 「둘 잔」.

desc: Dates are read using Sino-Korean numbers. Days of the week attach 「요일」 to the day name.
care: June is pronounced 「유월」 (not 「육월」), and October is pronounced 「시월」 (not 「십월」).

desc: Hours are read in native Korean numbers, while minutes are read in Sino-Korean numbers.
care: Say 「세 시 삼십 분」, not 「삼 시 삼십 분」. 30 minutes can also be called 「반」.

desc: The most formal speech style. Used in presentations, meetings, news broadcasts, and when meeting someone for the first time.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㅂ니다」 / with final consonant + 「-습니다」
care: Questions end in 「-(스)ㅂ니까?」. Using this style with close friends sounds overly stiff.

desc: The most common everyday polite style. It sounds polite and soft, making it suitable for almost any daily situation.
form: After stems ending in 「ㅏ, ㅗ」: 「-아요」 / Other vowels: 「-어요」 / 「하다」 verbs: 「해요」
care: Raise your intonation at the end to make it a question without changing the word form, like 「먹어요?」.

desc: Used to talk about actions or states that have already ended in the past.
form: After stems ending in 「ㅏ, ㅗ」: 「-았어요」 / Other vowels: 「-었어요」 / 「하다」 verbs: 「했어요」
care: 「-았/었어요」 is for completed events. If an action or state is still ongoing right now, use 「-고 있어요」.

desc: Used to talk about future actions or plans that have already been decided.
form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 거예요」 / with final consonant + 「-을 거예요」
care: Pronounced as [-ㄹ 꺼에요] when spoken, but must always be written as 「거예요」.

desc: Indicates that an action is currently in progress right now.
care: Use 「-고 계세요」 for honored elders or teachers, as in 「선생님이 기다리고 계세요」.

desc: Used to emphasize that a past state or event is no longer true today.
care: The key meaning is that the present is different. For simple completed past events, 「-았/었어요」 is enough.

desc: Words that have their own distinct antonyms instead of taking the negative prefix 「안」.
care: Do not say 「안 알아요」 or 「안 있어요」. Use 「몰라요」 and 「없어요」 instead.

desc: Expresses simple negative action or your intention not to do something.
care: For compound verbs like 「공부하다」 (Noun + 「하다」), place 「안」 in the middle: 「공부 안 해요」, not 「안 공부해요」.

desc: Expresses that you want to do something but cannot due to lack of ability or circumstances.
care: 「안」 means choosing not to do something, while 「못」 means being unable to do it. Swapping them changes the meaning.

desc: Subject marker pointing out who or what performs the action. Often introduces new information.
form: Noun with final consonant + 「이」 / without final consonant + 「가」
care: While 「저는」 introduces yourself as the topic, 「제가」 specifically highlights you as the person who did the action.

desc: Topic marker used to introduce what you are talking about or to draw a contrast with something else.
form: Noun with final consonant + 「은」 / without final consonant + 「는」
care: Particularly natural for contrasting two things, as in 「커피는 좋아하는데 차는 안 좋아해요」.

desc: Object marker indicating the target of an action.
form: Noun with final consonant + 「을」 / without final consonant + 「를」
care: Frequently dropped in casual spoken Korean. Saying 「밥 먹었어요?」 sounds more natural.

desc: Possessive marker indicating ownership or belonging.
care: It is much more natural to shorten 「나의」 to 「내」 and 「저의」 to 「제」.

desc: Indicates the location where something exists or the time when an event occurs.
care: Use 「에」 for static location of existence, and 「에서」 for dynamic action: 「집에 있어요 / 집에서 일해요」.

desc: Indicates a destination you are heading toward, or marks a unit of measurement/price.
care: The 「에」 in 「학교에 가요」 (direction) and in 「한 개에 천 원」 (unit) share the same spelling but serve different functions.

desc: Expresses 'from where to where' for locations, and 'from when to when' for time.
care: Use 「에서」 for starting locations and 「부터」 for starting points in time: 「아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지」.

desc: Particle meaning 'also' or 'too', indicating addition or inclusion.
care: When 「도」 is attached, particles like 「이/가」, 「은/는」, and 「을/를」 are dropped. Say 「저도」, not 「저는도」.

desc: Particle meaning 'only' or 'just', indicating exclusivity.
care: 「만」 replaces subject and object markers. It is also commonly used in polite requests like 「잠깐만요」.

desc: Indicates a tool, method, direction, or material used.
form: Noun without final consonant or ending in 「ㄹ」 + 「로」 / other consonants + 「으로」
care: Nouns ending in 「ㄹ」 take 「로」 without 「으」. Say 「연필로」, not 「연필으로」.

desc: Particle expressing an option between choices, meaning 'or'.
form: Noun with final consonant + 「이나」 / without final consonant + 「나」
care: Use 「-거나」 to connect verbs and 「(이)나」 to connect nouns.

desc: Attached to numbers to express surprise that an amount is more than expected.
care: When an amount is disappointingly small, use 「밖에」 instead. Compare with 「세 시간밖에 못 잤어요」.

desc: Attached to nouns to indicate an approximation or estimate.
care: Placing 「한」 before the noun makes it sound even more natural: 「한 시간쯤」.

desc: Connects two actions or states side by side, or lists sequential actions.
care: The subjects in both clauses can be different, as in 「저는 자고 동생은 공부했어요」.

desc: Smoothly connects contrasting clauses. It sounds far more natural in conversation than 「-지만」.
care: While 「-지만」 creates a sharp contrast, 「-는데」 introduces a gentle contrast and is much more common in speech.

desc: Expresses that the first action is completed and directly connected to the following action.
care: 「-고」 merely lists actions, while 「-아/어서」 links them sequentially. 「친구를 만나고 밥을 먹었어요」 implies eating separately.

desc: Indicates that someone is in the middle of doing an action right now.
care: Similar in meaning to 「-고 있다」, but 「-는 중」 sounds slightly more formal or stiff.

desc: Used to state how much time has passed since doing an action.
care: Followed by verbs like 「되다, 지나다, 넘다」. Distinct from the clause connector 「-는지」 (checking information).

desc: Expresses knowing or not knowing how to do something as a learned skill.
form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 줄」 / with final consonant + 「-을 줄」 + 「알다/모르다」
care: Used for learned skills. Being unable to do something due to external circumstances requires 「-(으)ㄹ 수 없다」.

desc: A polite way to tell or ask someone not to do something.
care: Cannot attach to adjectives. Phrases like 「예쁘지 마세요」 are incorrect.

desc: Expresses necessity or obligation, meaning one must do something.
care: 「되다」 is more common in spoken Korean, while 「하다」 fits written Korean better. Their meanings are identical.

desc: Used to give permission, meaning it is okay to do something.
care: Very frequently used when asking for permission. 「-아/어도 괜찮아요」 carries the same meaning.

desc: Used to prohibit an action, stating that one must not do it.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-면」 / with final consonant + 「-으면」 + 「안 되다」
care: While 「-지 마세요」 directly asks someone to stop, this form explains a prohibition or rule.

desc: Expresses how much time or money it takes to do something.
care: Use 「걸리다」 for time and 「들다」 for money. Leave a space before 「데」.

desc: Used to ask for confirmation about something you already know. Shortened to 「-죠?」 in speech.
care: Used to seek agreement or confirm facts, not to ask for brand-new information.

desc: Expresses a realization or exclamation upon learning something you did not know before.
care: Used for newly discovered facts. It sounds unnatural for things you already knew.

desc: Expresses spontaneous admiration or reaction to what you are currently seeing or feeling directly.
care: While 「-군요」 marks realization, 「-네요」 shares an immediate impression. It is much more common in speech.

desc: Used to ask questions softly. It sounds more cautious and gentle than 「-아/어요?」.
care: Well suited for first meetings or formal inquiries.

desc: Leaves the sentence open to create a lingering nuance. Used to decline softly or express mild surprise.
care: Sounds gentle because it avoids blunt conclusions. Especially common when declining something.

desc: Quotes someone's exact words directly as they were spoken.
care: Keep the words inside the quotation marks exactly as they were spoken without changing them.

desc: Paraphrases and reports what you heard in your own words.
care: The form splits into four types based on sentence kind. Telling these four apart is key.

desc: Shortened forms of indirect quotations used in spoken Korean.
care: Shortened forms are far more natural in speech. Use full forms in formal writing.

desc: When stems ending in 「ㅡ」 meet 「-아/어」, the vowel 「ㅡ」 drops.
care: Look at the vowel in the preceding syllable to choose between 「아」 and 「어」. 「바쁘다」 has 「ㅏ」, so it becomes 「바빠요」.

desc: The final consonant 「ㄹ」 drops before 「ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ」.
care: 「ㄹ」 also drops before 「-는」, as in 「사는 곳」 and 「만드는 법」.

desc: When the final consonant 「ㅂ」 meets a vowel, it changes to 「우」.
care: Only 「돕다」 and 「곱다」 change to 「오」 instead of 「우」: 「도와요」, 「고와요」.

desc: When the final consonant 「ㄷ」 meets a vowel, it changes to 「ㄹ」.
care: Verbs like 「받다」, 「닫다」, and 「믿다」 do not change: 「받아요」, 「닫아요」.

desc: When stems ending in 「르」 meet 「-아/어」, it changes into a double 「ㄹ」 (「ㄹㄹ」).
care: 「따르다」 and 「들르다」 follow regular 「ㅡ」 irregular rules: 「따라요」, 「들러요」.

desc: When the final consonant 「ㅅ」 meets a vowel, it drops.
care: Verbs like 「웃다」, 「씻다」, and 「벗다」 do not change: 「웃어요」, 「씻어요」.

desc: For adjectives with a final consonant 「ㅎ」, the 「ㅎ」 drops and the vowel changes.
care: Applies only to adjectives. Verbs like 「좋다」 and 「넣다」 do not change: 「좋아요」, 「넣어요」.

desc: Expresses an outward visual impression, meaning something looks or appears a certain way.
care: Attaches to adjectives. Distinct from 「-아/어 보다」 (to try doing something), which attaches to verbs.

desc: Expresses an inference based on what you observe. Used about other people or external situations.
form: Verb stem + 「-는 모양이다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 모양이다」 / Past tense + 「-(으)ㄴ 모양이다」
care: Do not use for your own direct actions or states. Saying 「제가 아픈 모양이에요」 is unnatural.

desc: Expresses worry or regret while guessing a likely situation.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 텐데」 / with final consonant + 「-을 텐데」
care: Usually followed by a concern or suggestion, as in 「배고플 텐데 이거 드세요」.

desc: Indicates that the speaker will do something, or presumes a situation, and tells the listener what to do.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 테니까」 / with final consonant + 「-을 테니까」
care: Followed by a command or suggestion. 「-(으)ㄹ 텐데」 expresses worry, while this provides a reason for action.

desc: Expresses a light guess about something you are not entirely sure of.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ걸요」 / with final consonant + 「-을걸요」
care: Resembles the regret expression 「-(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다」. Pronounce it with a slight upward intonation.

desc: Expresses that you did not expect something at all. Saying you knew means the opposite.
form: Past: 「-(으)ㄴ 줄」 / Present: 「-는 줄」 / Future: 「-(으)ㄹ 줄」 + 「알았다」 / 「몰랐다」
care: Distinct from ability in 「-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다」 (knowing how to do). This expresses an assumption.

desc: Expresses that there is a possibility that something might happen.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ지도」 / with final consonant + 「-을지도」 + 「모르다」
care: Gives a feeling of a roughly fifty-fifty chance. Frequently used when suggesting to pack an umbrella.

desc: Acknowledges one point first while stepping back to mention another contrasting aspect.
care: First admits the preceding fact before contrasting it. Softer than 「-지만」.

desc: Contrasts two opposing sides side by side, showing one is this way while the other is the opposite.
form: Verb stem + 「-는 반면에」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 반면에」
care: Used to compare two subjects side by side. Especially common in written Korean.

desc: Expresses that something happened despite expectations to the contrary.
form: Verb stem + 「-는데도」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ데도」 / Past tense + 「-았/었는데도」
care: While 「-아/어도」 is hypothetical, this describes a real, completed fact.

desc: Written narrative style used in newspapers, novels, diaries, and reports without addressing a specific listener.
care: Sounds like informal speech when spoken aloud. Strictly used in writing.

desc: Informal, casual speech style used with close friends or younger people.
care: Simply drop 「요」. Do not use with people you just met or with elders.

desc: Shares a reason that the listener does not know yet.
care: The reason comes at the end of the conversation, unlike 「-(으)니까」 where the cause comes first.

desc: Reminds the listener of a fact that they already know.
care: If used for something the listener does not know, it sounds argumentative. Use only for shared knowledge.

desc: Indicates that doing one action prevented another, resulting in a negative outcome.
care: The subject must be the same in both clauses, and past tense is not used before it: say 「하느라고」, not 「했느라고」.

desc: Indicates that an unexpected event occurred and caused a negative result.
care: Used for sudden situations outside your control. What follows is usually a negative outcome.

desc: Points out a cause in a blaming tone, stating it was the fault of that event.
form: Verb stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 탓에」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 탓에」 / Noun + 「탓에」
care: Do not use for positive events. For good results, use 「덕분에」.

desc: Mentions one of several reasons casually without listing them all.
care: Sounds more natural when paired with 「도」. Used when you choose not to list every single reason.

desc: Repeats what you heard in disbelief to ask for confirmation.
care: Used to ask back in surprise, or to re-confirm when you did not hear clearly.

desc: Passes on something you heard and asks for the listener's thoughts.
care: Used for things heard from others, not witnessed firsthand. Frequently followed by a question or suggestion.

desc: Expresses that doing a certain action resulted in a particular outcome or discovery.
care: The first clause is what you did, and the second is the result. The subjects are opposite to 「-더니」.

desc: Warns that continuing to do an action will eventually lead to a bad result.
care: Always followed by a negative outcome. Used to dissuade someone from doing something.

desc: Indicates that, all things considered, a situation is practically equivalent to something.
form: Verb stem + 「-는 셈이다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 셈이다」
care: Means it is not strictly identical, but it can be considered practically the same.

desc: Indicates doing an action in advance and maintaining that resulting state.
care: Almost identical to 「-아/어 두다」, but 「놓다」 is slightly more colloquial.

desc: Indicates doing an action in advance for future use or purpose.
care: Carries a sense of keeping the state longer than 「놓다」, as in 「보관해 두다」.

desc: Indicates doing another action while maintaining the preceding state unchanged.
form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄴ 채로」 / with final consonant + 「-은 채로」
care: Usually used for situations where doing so is improper, as in 「불을 켠 채로 잤어요」.

desc: Means doing something exactly as it is, or immediately after an action occurs.
form: Verb stem + 「-는 대로」 / Past tense + 「-(으)ㄴ 대로」 / Noun + 「대로」
care: Also used to mean 'as soon as', as in 「도착하는 대로 연락할게요」.

desc: States that something leans toward a certain side rather than making a definitive claim.
form: Verb stem + 「-는 편이다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 편이다」
care: Avoids blunt assertions, making it very common in self-introductions.

desc: Attaches to a noun to create an adjective meaning having that quality or impression.
care: While 「답다」 means fitting the qualifications, 「스럽다」 means giving off that impression.

desc: Attaches to a noun to indicate being truly worthy of or matching its name.
care: Mainly used for praise. 「어른답다」 means behaving up to the qualifications of an adult.

desc: Emphasizes the extreme degree of a state or action beyond description.
care: Omitting the leading word 「얼마나」 changes the meaning. Always use them together.

desc: Expresses that there is no other choice or alternative but to do that action.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 수밖에」 / with final consonant + 「-을 수밖에」 + 「없다」
care: Means there is no other way. Used when making excuses or explaining inevitable circumstances.

desc: Expresses that something is only that one thing and nothing more.
form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 뿐」 / with final consonant + 「-을 뿐」 + 「이다」
care: Used to speak modestly or to draw a clear line.

desc: Indicates a purpose or goal, meaning 'so that' a certain state or action is achieved.
care: Shorter and more casual than 「-도록」, making it much more frequent in spoken Korean.

desc: Indicates that an action was completed and then reversed to the opposite state.
care: While 「-다가」 means interrupted midway, this occurs after full completion. A reverse action follows.

desc: Expresses completing an action entirely, accompanied by feelings of relief or regret.
care: Carries two nuances: relief in 「끝내 버렸다」, or regret in 「잃어버렸다」.

desc: Expresses that a situation ended up happening in the end, with strong lingering regret.
care: Carries deeper regret than 「-아/어 버리다」. Used when things did not turn out as desired.

desc: Expresses that doing or not doing the action makes no difference, so it is useless.
form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-나 마나」 / with final consonant + 「-으나 마나」
care: Used when the result is completely predictable. That obvious result follows in the next clause.

desc: Expresses that even if you try doing the action, it will be useless or in vain.
care: Followed by words indicating futility. More colloquial than 「-(으)나 마나」.

desc: Expresses regret about a past situation, imagining what would have happened if things went differently.
care: Used for past events that cannot be changed. Commonly followed by 「-았/었을 텐데」.

desc: Indicates that something almost happened, but ultimately did not occur in reality.
form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 뻔하다」 / with final consonant + 「-을 뻔하다」
care: Used for things that did not actually occur. Always used in the past tense.

desc: Expresses personal regret, wishing that you had done a particular action.
form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ걸」 / with final consonant + 「-을걸」 + 「그랬다」
care: Shares a similar form with guessing 「-(으)ㄹ걸요」. Distinguish it by the ending 「그랬다」.

desc: Expresses regret that you should have done something, but failed to do so.
care: Carries a heavier sense of admitting your own fault than 「-(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다」.

desc: Expresses a repeated habit or routine that you do from time to time.
care: Use the past form 「-곤 했다」 for past habits: 「어릴 때 자주 놀곤 했어요」.

desc: Used to modestly deflect a compliment or apologize in a humble way.
care: Used as a humble reply when receiving a compliment. Speak in a gentle tone.

desc: Indicates pretending to do or be something that is not true in reality.
form: Verb stem + 「-는 척하다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 척하다」 / Past tense + 「-(으)ㄴ 척하다」
care: While 「-는 것 같다」 is a guess, 「-는 척하다」 is an intentional pretense.

desc: Indicates that choosing the latter option is better than doing the former.
care: Not used with the past tense marker 「-았/었-」.

desc: Expresses choosing a better alternative since things have already ended up this way.
care: Presupposes a predetermined situation. 「-느니」 compares two actions side by side.

desc: Indicates that the outcome remains the same regardless of which option is chosen.
care: Used by repeating the same word or pairing antonyms together.

desc: Used to rephrase a statement, indicating that the latter expression is more accurate than the former.
care: Ideal for softening and refining the other person's wording.

desc: A colloquial particle pointing to the person spoken to. Used among closer acquaintances than 「에게」.
care: Used only in spoken Korean. Use 「에게」 in formal settings.

desc: Used to emphasize and reiterate what you already said.
care: Repeats the same statement to express frustration or strong emphasis.

desc: Used to ask the listener for confirmation regarding a fact you heard.
care: Since it asks for confirmation, pronounce it with a rising intonation at the end.

desc: A formal expression used to state the source of information.
care: The following sentence naturally ends with a quoted citation form.

desc: A written nominalizer that turns sentences into noun forms, commonly used in public notices and reports.
care: Used in written public notices and reports. In spoken Korean, 「-는 것」 is more natural.

desc: Used in formal contexts to refer to the preceding content and continue the statement.
care: Mainly used in formal written documents.
